extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, philosophers, and scholarly readers of the book (readers interested in authorial responses and critical method)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles, embedded in the author's reply and appendix, about how critics should interpret, judge, and respond to an author's work — and how an author may legitimately alter or suppress passages to avoid misrepresentation of their argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge author by latest expression
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usual in literary criticism to judge an author by the latest expression of his views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts that critics should give weight to an author's most recent statements; if an author has corrected an earlier error, it is 'nothing but fair' to allow him the benefit of that correction. This is presented as a customary standard of fairness in literary criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow the author benefit of corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: It is commonly thought nothing but fair that if he has made an error ... he should be allowed the benefit of any correction he makes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should not continue to judge an author solely by past formulations if the author has publicly revised or corrected them. Anti-pattern: insisting on past alleged errors after the author has remedied them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ideological or partisan motives in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic ought not to be moved by sectarian or 'doing God service' motives to treat an author's changed expression unfairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns against critics who, from a desire to score points for their creed, refuse generous dealing. Criticism driven by doctrinal zeal is framed as ethically suspect and likely to misrepresent the opponent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate representation of the author's claims (distinguish law from existence-claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attribute to an author statements he has not made — e.g., asserting 'that gravitation is a necessary result of the laws of space' when the author only claimed a law of variation is deducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics must carefully parse what the author actually asserts. The page gives a concrete anti-pattern: transforming a claim about a law (the form or law governing a force) into a claim about the existence of a particular cosmic force, then deriving absurd consequences. Guidance: distinguish claims about form/law from claims about ontological existence when quoting or criticizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress or replace illustrative passages only to remove misrepresentation risks
rubrics_metrics.description: It is legitimate to remove or substitute an illustration if it becomes a 'stumbling-block' by inviting repeated misrepresentation, provided the rest of the chapter and its argument remain unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains his motive for suppressing/replacing a passage: another writer had misrepresented that illustration and based animadversions on the misrepresentation. Removing the passage can be a defensive editorial choice to prevent opponents from evading the chapter's general argument by opening side issues that are not essential. Scoring note: acceptable so long as the substantive argument is unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics should compare their strictures with the original work
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers who 'take the pains to read my strictures, and compare them with the statements of the work to which they are a reply, will find the effort repaid by a clearer apprehension of the topics in debate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit guidance to critics and readers: perform side-by-side comparison between criticisms and the original text. Anti-pattern: relying on paraphrase, hearsay, or misread secondary accounts rather than direct comparison; such practice is likely to lead to misapprehension rather than clarity.
